transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-10
Time: 13:47 UTC
Duration: 62m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Owen (Redwood SE), Janelle (Product), Marina (Helix Head of ML), Diego (Helix Platform), Samir (CTO), Ravi (SRE)

Auto-summary: Walkthrough of Redwood API parity for Helix's multi-vendor stack. Clarify model mappings, streaming differences, and operational tasks for a POC.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Marina (Helix): Marina here.
[00:10] Diego: Diego.
[00:12] Samir: Samir.
[00:14] Ravi: Ravi on SRE.
[00:16] Owen (Redwood SE): Owen here.
[00:18] Janelle (Product): Janelle here.
[00:20] Maya: Great. We're booked for an hour, we have a packed agenda but mostly demo + parity mapping. We'll try to leave 10 minutes for security. Owen, do you want to start with the model map?
[00:34] Owen: Sure. So high level, Helix's current stack is a mix of OpenAI for chat endpoints, Anthropic for safety-tilted completions, and Together for some local cost-sensitive workloads. The goal we heard is to unify to a single Redwood API layer while preserving behavior and not regressing latency or cost.
[01:02] Marina: Exactly. We have streaming hooks and function calls for some real-time features so parity there is important. Also retention and data residency — we need private deployment for some PII workloads.
[01:20] Owen: Totally. On the model side, we map OpenAI gpt-4 style calls to Redwood's curated equivalents — model names differ, tokenizers can differ subtly. For Anthropic, we recommended semantic-equivalent models with tuned system prompts; Together models are often quantized variants we can host under Dedicated or Private.
[01:45] Diego: Tokenization caveats — can you expand? We saw in a few tests the token counts shifted and cost estimates changed.
[01:53] Owen: Yeah, good callout. Redwood exposes tokenizer info in the model metadata but there are micro-differences; for a strict cost parity we suggest running a tokenization diff on a representative prompt set. We'll provide a small parity tool.
[02:15] Marina: That would help. Also, function-calling differences... in Anthropic we use a schema-first flow, and OpenAI does function_call. How does Redwood handle those?
[02:29] Janelle: Redwood supports both patterns — you can stream structured outputs and do function-calling via the API. There are SDK helpers we demo in the console. Small differences: for some models the structured output shape requires explicit parse modes; we'll show examples.
[02:50] Maya: We'll demo the console flow now — Owen, take it away.
[03:05] [Screen share noise, brief pause]
[03:15] Owen: Ok, console landing page. Top-left you see the model catalog, and we annotate compatibility notes with OpenAI/Anthropic/Together equivalents. Click into a model profile — note the tokenization tab and the streaming knobs.
[03:42] Marina: That tokenization tab is new to us — nice. Does it show per-token cost?
[03:47] Owen: We show unit token cost per model and an estimate based on your sample set if you upload a small corpus. The Optimize tab recommends batching sizes and quantization levels based on your latency SLO.
[04:05] Samir: Latency SLO — can you show an example? Our production p99 needs to be sub 180ms for short completions.
[04:16] Owen: Sure — here's a p99 dashboard for a similar workload. For small completion length we rely on single-token-fanout optimizations, GPU kernels, and prefix caching. For p99 under 180ms you may need Dedicated pools in region. We'll run a POC to validate.
[04:40] Marina: What's the cost delta if we move Dedicated vs hosted?
[04:46] Maya: There are two levers: per-token unit economics and reserved capacity. Hosted is simplest but at scale Dedicated reduces per-token cost and gives you isolation. We'll share a model showing break-even at your estimated QPS.
[05:05] Diego: How about private deployment? We have some regulated datasets that cannot leave our VPC.
[05:11] Owen: Redwood Private supports a customer-controlled control plane and optional on-prem inference. We support VPC peering, private endpoints, and KMS/HSM integrations. Audit logs are shipped to your SIEM.
[05:30] Ravi: For the VPC path, we need to understand egress and peering details — we use strict egress rules.
[05:35] Janelle: We'll provide the architecture diagram and an ops runbook with the exact CIDR and firewall ports. Also, there are offline PCI/no-egress patterns we can support with an on-prem appliance.
[05:52] Marina: Good. Can you walk through a parity example — say an OpenAI chat call that uses streaming + function call + stop sequences?
[06:01] Owen: Absolutely. Example 1: OpenAI chat completion with function_call: "get_order_status". On Redwood you'd call the chat endpoint, include the function schema in the same payload, and set streaming to true. The SDK will emit partial JSON deltas; we have a small helper to reconstruct the final function call payload.
[06:26] Diego: Any gotchas for Together models we self-host? We rely on 4-bit quantization to save costs.
[06:33] Owen: Together-style quantized weights are supported in our Dedicated pools; kernel selection can change latency so we'll advise specific GPU families. Optimize recommendations will suggest 4-bit vs 8-bit based on your quality/perf tradeoff.
[06:52] Maya: Let me interject with a live demo of parity mapping spreadsheet — I uploaded a sample mapping earlier.
[07:00] [small typing sounds]
[07:10] Maya: Here: column A is current vendor + model, column B is Redwood equivalent, C is tokenizer delta notes, D is required rollout steps. Example: OpenAI gpt-4o -> Redwood-rx-4o, note: tokenization identical; rollout notes: update client to point to new base path, test streaming.
[07:36] Marina: We like having the rollout steps. How do canaries and rollbacks work in Redwood?
[07:42] Owen: Console supports canary routes: you can route X% of traffic to new model version, do A/B comparisons, and auto-fallback on error thresholds. We also keep per-route cost breakouts and token-level tracing for debugging.
[08:01] Samir: Token-level tracing — is that sensitive? We need to ensure we can redact or avoid storing PII.
[08:09] Janelle: Yes, you control retention and redaction policies. For Private deployments, logs can be pushed to your S3 with encryption and automatic redaction.
[08:20] Marina: What about evals — we need to ensure output quality parity.
[08:26] Owen: Redwood Optimize includes eval suites tied to your prompt set. You can run batch evals pre and post-migration; alerts fire if regressions exceed thresholds. We'll demo that in the POC.
[08:40] Diego: Ok can we talk about streaming semantics — we saw in Anthropic the delta chunks include partial tokens in a different shape. Will our client need changes?
[08:49] Owen: Potentially small changes. We provide SDK adapters for Node/Python that normalize streaming deltas into the common shape. If you prefer a drop-in replacement, we have a compatibility adapter that mimics OpenAI-style deltas.
[09:06] Marina: That sounds good. For authentication, we use SSO and fine-grained RBAC. How does Redwood integrate?
[09:14] Maya: We support SAML SSO, OIDC, SCIM for provisioning, and role-based permissions in the console. For API keys you can scope keys to routes and set per-key quotas.
[09:30] Ravi: KMS integration details? We use AWS KMS with custom rotation.
[09:35] Owen: We have guides for AWS KMS and HSM workflows; for Private you can plug directly into your KMS and keys never leave your account.
[09:46] Samir: Can we cover a quick POC plan? Timeline and success criteria?
[09:51] Maya: Proposed POC: week 1: run tokenization diffs and small fidelity tests; week 2: provisioning Dedicated pool + run latency and p99 benchmarks; week 3: run eval suites and A/B traffic at 10% for two days. Success criteria: p99 within 20% of current, no functional regressions in evals, and cost within projected threshold.
[10:16] Marina: 20% p99 delta is acceptable if cost improves.
[10:20] Diego: Who owns the benchmark infra?
[10:22] Owen: Redwood will run initial benchmarks in our staging, but we'll need you to run a final benchmark in your VPC or a peered environment to validate networking.
[10:34] [Longer pause, some side conversation about scheduling]
[11:10] Maya: Quick question from sales ops — any procurement constraints?
[11:13] Samir: We have a procurement window for Q4, but technically we can start a pilot earlier under the eval agreement. Legal will want SOC2, data processing agreement, and liability clauses.
[11:28] Maya: We'll get those docs in the package.
[11:32] Marina: On the console tour — can you show the route editor and how to pin a model version?
[11:38] Owen: Sure — route editor here. Create a route, attach policy: latency SLO 200ms, fallback to a cheaper model if p99 breached, and pin a model version. You can also set per-route caching TTLs for prefix caching.
[11:56] Diego: Prefix caching — how does that interact with KV cache for chat sessions?
[12:01] Owen: We maintain a KV cache for key/value states; prefix caching stores repeated prefixes to avoid recomputation. It works well for multi-turn chat where the preamble is constant. There's a cache invalidation strategy exposed in the API.
[12:20] Marina: Any specific SDK changes we should expect? We use a small wrapper around OpenAI client.
[12:27] Owen: If you use our compatibility adapter, changes are minimal: swap base URL, keep most call shapes. If you want to hit Redwood native features (Optimize hints, console hooks), you'll want to adopt our SDK which is quick (a couple extra lines).
[12:41] Maya: Let's demo a short migration code snippet — Node example for streaming chat.
[12:49] [typing]
[13:00] Owen: Code: set up client with apiKey, call client.chat.stream with messages, include functions schema. The adapter will expose onDelta callbacks.
[13:11] Marina: That looks straightforward. For function outputs we need deterministic JSON structure — how do you guarantee that?
[13:18] Janelle: Our structured output mode enforces JSON schema and can auto-retry if parse errors exceed threshold. For non-deterministic models we recommend schema enforcement at the SDK level.
[13:32] Samir: Security again — audit logs retention and access control. Can we limit which engineers see full transcripts?
[13:39] Janelle: Yes, RBAC scoping plus field redaction. For example, only the compliance role can view full transcripts; devs see redacted traces.
[13:49] Diego: Billing questions: token trace is powerful but will it blow up our billing export?
[13:55] Maya: Token-level trace is optional and can be sampled. We also surface aggregated token cost per route to reduce noise.
[14:06] Marina: Ok, let's move to the Optimize recommendations — batching/quantization.
[14:11] Owen: In Optimize you feed a representative latency distribution and we'll suggest batch sizes. For lower latency, smaller batches or single-shot with caching is better; for throughput you can increase batching. Quantization: 4-bit gives big cost win, we recommend running quality evals.
[14:33] Marina: Will quantization require changes to our prompt engineering?
[14:37] Owen: Sometimes; slight prompt tuning may be needed. Our eval harness helps identify prompts that degrade.
[14:46] Ravi: For the POC bench, what metrics will you deliver?
[14:50] Owen: p50/p95/p99, cost per 1k tokens, end-to-end wall time including network, per-route error rates, and eval quality scores.
[15:01] Maya: Ok, quick recap and next steps.
[15:05] Maya: Action items — I will send the parity spreadsheet and pricing by Monday. Owen will run an initial latency bench after we get your prompt set. Marina and Diego will share the traffic profile. Diego will set up VPC peering invite. Janelle will attach the security docs.
[15:25] Marina: Sounds good. Anything else?
[15:28] Samir: One more question — operator training. How long until our team can run console rollouts?
[15:34] Janelle: Typical ramp is 2-3 days of hands-on training; we can include a 4-hour workshop during the POC.
[15:41] Marina: Great.
[15:43] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with an invite to POC kickoff.
[15:48] Diego: Thanks.

[End summary notes] 
- POC plan agreed: token diffs -> staging benchmarks -> evals -> 10% canary.
- Security package and runbook to be shared.
- Parity mapping spreadsheet will be the source of truth for model names and rollout steps.

Transcript artifacts/notes: there were a few transcription errors around product names (e.g., 'Redwood Dedciated' misheard once) and some overlapping speech at the end of the demo.
